additionalFinding_A1_C8_blogOrder.concern: lib/storage.ts getPublishedBlogPosts() / getAllBlogPosts() order by created_at desc with no tiebreaker; order among posts sharing the same created_at is formally unspecified by SQL and could differ between Replit and the restored Neon copy.
additionalFinding_A1_C8_blogOrder.method: Compared this local build's GET /api/blog slug order (server on restored blog-tables.dump) against docs/migration/.scratch/raw-baseline/_api_blog.bin (Replit's raw P1.3 live baseline of the same endpoint), programmatically (slug list equality, not by inspection).
additionalFinding_A1_C8_blogOrder.result: MATCH: both are 172-element arrays (171 DB rows + 1 code-level fallback), identical set of slugs, and the slug sequence is identical element-for-element (index-by-index list equality confirmed true).
additionalFinding_A1_C8_blogOrder.tieAnalysis: blog_posts.created_at is day-granularity so many rows tie (7 rows on 2021-12-23, 5 on 2024-06-22, 5 on 2024-08-04, several groups of 3-4, etc.). Despite these ties, order matched exactly, consistent with round 1's conclusion: a straight COPY-based data-only restore preserves the source's physical/insertion row order, and Postgres returns tied rows in that same heap-scan order on both sides absent an ORDER BY tiebreaker. This is a property of the current restore path, not a guarantee once Neon receives its own inserts, updates, autovacuum, or a different restore mechanism (e.g. the real P4 full pg_dump/restore).
additionalFinding_A1_C8_blogOrder.verdict: MATCH (no discrepancy to record this round either); the underlying nondeterminism risk in lib/storage.ts (no explicit tiebreaker such as `, asc(blogPosts.id)`) remains real for the production data path and is flagged for the record only. No code change made per instructions.
